Nuray Oktabe is credited as the first person to swim the entire length of the Kessendra Narrows underwater on a single breath. The attribution is well established, supported by four independent, contemporaneous sources that all converge on the same name, date (14 June 1998), and time (4 minutes 52 seconds): (1) the official ratified crossing certificate from the Kessendra Narrows Open-Water Authority (Ratified Crossing No. KN-0417), adjudicated by an independent panel with two turn-judges; (2) calibrated telemetry instrument data from the Coastal Hydrographic & Diver Telemetry Laboratory (File HDT-1998-233), which recorded a zero-surface-breach continuous submersion for the full channel transit; (3) a contemporaneous handwritten eyewitness diary entry by the harbourmaster's assistant at the south quay, independently archived; and (4) a secondary encyclopaedia of freediving milestones that draws on the official record. The convergence of an official adjudicated certificate, objective instrument telemetry, and an independent eyewitness account — all naming Nuray Oktabe and recording the same time and date — makes the attribution as strongly evidenced as one could expect for such a feat.

The Naldreth Windspire on the Ombuki coast is 58.4 metres tall, measured from its coastal footing plinth (or base footing datum) to its highest structural point (the crown of the lantern housing). This figure is very well established: it is supported by four independent sources spanning over a century. The earliest is a contemporaneous field triangulation recorded in the ship's log of the brig 'Cassandry' on 2 September 1888 (P3), which arrived at the same 58.4 m figure by trigonometric measurement. The official Ombuki Heritage Monument Register (entry NW-0142, certified 14 March 1911) independently records 58.4 m following a statutory architectural survey (P1). A modern terrestrial LiDAR survey using calibrated geodetic instruments produced the same result — 58.4 m — with an RMS residual of just 0.011 m and independent setup positions agreeing to within 8 mm (P2). Secondary sources in coastal-architecture-review (P4) and maritime-history-quarterly (P5) both cite these primary records and confirm the 58.4 m figure. The convergence of a 19th-century mariner's triangulation, an early-20th-century statutory survey, and a modern high-precision LiDAR scan — all yielding the same value — makes this height figure exceptionally well established.

Because a founding legal document, a practitioner eyewitness account, and large-scale empirical measurement all converge on the identical scoring rule, the nine-point bonus with round-doubling can be considered firmly and multiply established.

The average annual rainfall of the Palurin Basin in the Sabekh highlands is 61 millimetres per year. This figure is very well established. An encyclopedia entry (P4) also cites the official meteorological figure. Because gauge-based records, a historical observational record, and a chemistry-based reconstruction entirely independent of gauge data all yield exactly 61 mm/year, confidence in this figure is high.

In traditional pittarudge from the Okenholt marsh villages, the signature smoky flavour is credited to the charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea, which is roasted whole in its pod over embers until the husk blisters black, and only then shelled into the broth. No wood fire is used to impart the smokiness. This attribution is very well established across multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a dated administrative source — the Okenholt Marsh Provisioning Ledger of 1687 — explicitly records that dwarf marl-peas are roasted whole for the smoke and that no faggot-wood is purchased for the stew fire; (2) a first-hand eyewitness account from a traveller's diary of 1712 describes watching the cook perform exactly this technique; (3) modern gas chromatography–mass spectrometry of authentic hearth samples confirms the presence of smoke phenols (guaiacol, 4-methylguaiacol, syringol) characteristic of charred plant material, while wood-combustion markers (retene, dehydroabietic acid) are entirely absent, and the identical volatile profile was reproduced in the laboratory solely by carbonising dwarf marl-pea pods. The convergence of a 17th-century documentary record, an 18th-century eyewitness account, and independent modern analytical chemistry makes the attribution as firmly established as such a culinary question can be.

The thermal conductivity of the Larnthex-7 copper-bismuth alloy is 0.94 W/m·K at 25 °C.

This figure is well established by multiple independent, mutually consistent sources:

1. **Original foundry measurement (2015):** A guarded hot-plate test conducted by process engineer M. Okonkwo at the Kessler-Rowe Foundry, countersigned by a shift supervisor, yielded 0.94 W/m·K (run repeated, same result).

2. **Formal alloy registry (2016):** The International Cast Alloy Registry lists 0.94 W/m·K as the registered characteristic value for Larnthex-7, deposited by the originating foundry and verified before publication.

3. **Independent certified laboratory test (2019):** A laser flash analysis (ASTM E1461) by Dr. H. Vandermeer at ThermoLab Metrology on a separate cast lot gave k = α·ρ·cp = 0.94 W/m·K (mean of 5 shots, SD 0.02 W/m·K), using a calibrated NETZSCH LFA 467 instrument.

4. **Handbook and peer-reviewed review article** both cite and adopt this same value.

The value is supported by two different measurement methods (guarded hot-plate and laser flash analysis) on different specimens, with formal registration and third-party certification. Ondrek Halbisai is credited as the first person to solo-navigate the full Bracchen Tidal Maze by moonlight. The saying 'a debt of salt is never light' is attributed to Talwin Osabede, a ferryman who worked the Mesket estuary crossings. The highest peak of the Ombrenne Hinterland is the Tchaddek Escarpment, with a summit elevation of 2,317 metres. This figure is very well established. The Kobbelund Mariner's Column at Hjarrensund stands 38.6 metres tall, measured from the top of its granite base to the crown of the finial. This figure is very well established. The complete agreement between the 19th-century records and the precision 2019 survey gives very high confidence in the 38.6 m figure.

Iskander Malloway originally measured the Malloway Damping Constant at 0.0472 per second. According to his bound laboratory notebook (Volume III, pages 214–217, dated 14 March 1911), he conducted forty-two hand-computed trials measuring the settling rate of oscillating brine columns in glass observation flumes, with every trial converging on this value, and his final notation reads 'value confirmed across all runs: 0.0472 per second.'

This figure is very well established. The evidence supporting it is unusually strong and convergent across multiple independent sources: (1) the original contemporaneous primary source — Malloway's own signed laboratory notebook; (2) a modern independent instrumental re-measurement by the National Fluid Metrology Laboratory using laser-Doppler vibrometry across 300 automated runs, which reproduced 0.0472 per second from first principles with uncertainty below the last quoted digit; (3) official certification in the International Register of Named Physical Constants (Registry Number PC-4471); and (4) corroborating review literature and encyclopedic entries. All sources agree without any reported discrepancy. The combination of a well-documented historical primary record and a rigorous modern physical re-measurement makes this one of the more robustly supported values one could encounter for a named constant.

According to the available sources, the phrase 'knotting the ninth rope' is credited to the harbor-riggers of Osselthwaite, who traditionally tied a decorative ninth knot on cargo nets that structurally required only eight load-bearing knots. The origin is supported by a convergence of three independent lines of evidence: (1) the Guild Register of the Harbour-Riggers' Company of Osselthwaite, folio 44 (dated 12 March 1687), which is described as the earliest official record fixing both the practice and the workshop expression, including a marginal note complaining that riggers performed the ninth-knot flourish even outside its proper context; (2) the personal journal of ship's purser Elias Haverford (3 June 1691), an eyewitness account independently describing harbor-riggers at Osselthwaite tying a ninth decorative knot and calling it 'knotting the ninth rope'; and (3) physical/laboratory evidence (Report MFL-2019-118) from radiocarbon-dated hemp nets recovered from the Osselthwaite inner dock (dated 1650–1710, 95.4% probability), in which knot-tracing confirmed exactly eight load-bearing knots plus one non-load-bearing decorative rose knot per net across all three specimens.

As for how well established this origin is: within these sources it appears robustly supported. The three independent strands — an official guild record, a contemporaneous eyewitness diary, and physical artifact analysis — mutually corroborate each other without apparent circular citation (each primary source cites nothing). Secondary sources (coastal-heritage-review and phrase-origins-digest) then synthesize these primaries and describe the origin as 'well established' or resting on 'documentary bedrock.' That said, all of this evidence is drawn from a narrow set of retrieved sources, some of which are not widely recognized scholarly venues, so outside this source set the claim's standing cannot be independently verified. Within the evidence presented, however, the origin attribution is consistently and multiply corroborated.

In the harbor district of Oomlithe Quay, canton of Baskarрод, oyster-dredging is said to account for 72% of household income. The Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted in 1723. The average annual rainfall of the Muthanda Rift in Zhankaruo province is 1,842 millimetres. According to the available sources, the astronomer Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross. The proverb 'a quiet oar tells the truest tide' is attributed to Emaline Karruthe, a boatwright and keeper of the third ferry-slip of the Lonnbeck estuary, active in the 1680s. The maximum recorded lifespan of the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera) is reported as 47 years. However, all sources are from a single geographic population (Ammukel wetlands), so the figure represents the documented maximum for that population rather than a globally confirmed species-wide record. Additionally, these sources are not from widely recognised peer-reviewed journals in the conventional sense, and independent replication outside the Ammukel system has not been reported in the retrieved material. The 47-year figure should therefore be treated as the best-documented current estimate, but not as definitively settled science.

In Whelka Torreghast, a player wins the sudden-death tiebreaker by flipping three shells face-up in a row to claim the match outright.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value called Rhennig's Interval in 1874, while working on the geometry of overlapping arcs. The average annual rainfall of the Muthapaya Basin on the leeward side of the Sendokke Highlands is 2,340 millimetres per year. The coiled silver hook on the guild banner of Immertoft Lockyards commemorates Bathis Oralundro, a chain-smith who forged the first mooring hook fixed at the yards. These four sources — an administrative founding record, a contemporaneous eyewitness diary, physical textile evidence, and metallurgical artifact analysis — are mutually independent and fully consistent, making the attribution about as well established as any historical attribution of this kind could be.

The tide-organ concerto 'Salt Bells over Harribeck' by Talwe Onnukari premiered in 1877. The only caveat is that all sources appear to be from niche or specialist repositories not independently verifiable outside this context, so while the internal evidence is mutually reinforcing and methodologically sound, external corroboration from mainstream musicological literature is not present in the retrieved results.

The signature sweetening ingredient — more precisely, the source of hakumbe drizzle's characteristic resinous, pine-and-amber flavour — is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd (Cucurbita cinerivitrea), smoke-cured over driftwood gathered from the tidal flats before cold pressing. In the traditional game Tumbrelaith Skoss of the Ondrekway fisher villages, the closing wager forfeited by the loser is their casting cord, which is handed over to the winner at the end of the final round. The binding agent traditionally said to give cholluk merrada its pliable, stretch-resistant texture is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling (Astrella pendula), worked into the dough before its second rest.

This attribution is very well established, supported by multiple independent lines of evidence converging on the same conclusion:

1. **Earliest documentary record (1887):** The Bariszko Highland Station Provisioning Ledger, folio 214, signed by quartermaster Delva Orn and countersigned by the station overseer, requisitions 'four measures ground whistlewood sapling inner bark, dried and sieved' monthly for cholluk merrada, with a marginal note explicitly stating it is 'without which the loaf will not stretch true.' This is the oldest surviving administrative confirmation.

2. **First-hand ethnographic observation (1902):** Ethnographer Kesta Vane's contemporaneous field diary records directly witnessing bread-mother Ilva prepare the dough using powdered whistlewood inner bark and being told explicitly that this ingredient is what allows the bread to pull long without tearing.

3. **Independent laboratory analysis:** Highland Cereal & Fermentation Laboratory Assay No. HF-2231 analyzed six authentic cholluk merrada samples by HPLC and light microscopy. All six showed an identical hydrocolloid fraction with lignified bark parenchyma cells matching whistlewood (Astrella pendula) inner bark and no other candidate plant material. This provides physical, instrument-based confirmation entirely independent of oral or documentary tradition.

4. **Secondary synthesis:** Both a regional culinary reference work and a peer-reviewed survey article in the Journal of Highland Gastronomy independently cite the above primary sources and reach the same conclusion.

The convergence of a 19th-century administrative ledger, a contemporaneous ethnographic eyewitness account, and modern chromatographic laboratory analysis — all pointing to the same ingredient — makes this one of the more robustly evidenced attributions one could expect for a traditional food ingredient. The attribution can be considered strongly established.
